issues.body: PrivacyBudget::would_exceed still compares delta_spent + params.delta against delta_total + BUDGET_EPS_TOL, where BUDGET_EPS_TOL is 1e-12. Thus PrivacyBudget::new(..., 0.0), documented to refuse every non-trivial query, can accept a valid DpParams with positive delta <= 1e-12; more generally the ledger can authorize spend up to 1e-12 beyond delta_total. That absolute slack is material for cryptographic failure probabilities and breaks the claimed fail-closed basic-composition invariant. None of the added ledger-path tests covers a zero or sub-1e-12 delta budget.
issues.fix_hint: Remove fixed absolute tolerance from delta accounting and use a conservative comparison or representation that can never authorize delta spend above the configured total. Keep any epsilon rounding accommodation separate. Add a regression test using delta_total = 0 and a constructible DpParams with positive delta below 1e-12, plus a near-boundary small-delta composition test; both must refuse without mutating spend.
issues.title: Absolute tolerance still permits overspending small delta budgets

verdict.summary: Round 4 is stagnant: the round 3 major finding remains unchanged. PrivacyBudget::would_exceed still adds the fixed 1e-12 BUDGET_EPS_TOL to both epsilon_total and delta_total, so a zero delta budget can authorize a valid release with a positive delta at or below 1e-12, and small configured delta budgets can be overspent by the same absolute amount. The new ledger release tests use delta values of 1e-6 or larger and do not exercise this fail-closed boundary. Because the accountant still violates its documented basic-composition and zero-budget behavior on the delta axis, the change is not sound as scoped.
